[Hard-BPR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) directly addresses the main risk of mining negatives with the current network: high-scoring unobserved items can be false negatives, and standard BPR can apply harmful gradients. It modifies the objective for dynamic hard-negative sampling, reporting improved robustness on three datasets. [SL@K (KDD 2025)](https://jiawei-chen.github.io/paper/KDD25-SLK.pdf) offers a complementary direction: a sampled quantile estimates the top-K score threshold, producing a smooth NDCG@K surrogate without explicitly sorting the full catalog. Its reported gains include sequential-recommendation experiments, but do not establish improvement on this task’s sampled HR@10.

[CATS (SIGIR 2026)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) uses adaptive cluster-based sampling to balance informative negatives against false-negative risk, gradually reducing sampling from the positive item’s own cluster. Its clustering assumption is a heuristic, not proof that an item is negative. A [2024 sequential-recommendation sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compares random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive strategies; results depend on dataset characteristics, and aggregate accuracy can conceal popularity-band tradeoffs.

For NextItNet, these findings motivate a controlled single-model experiment: compare uniform multiple-negative training against negatives scored by the same network, then test a robust loss or stochastic selection from a hard-candidate pool. Exclude observed training positives; treat remaining false-negative protection as heuristic. Keep candidate counts and training budgets comparable, and separately ablate sampling and loss changes. Select using the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10; larger training margins alone provide no evidence of improved recommendation quality.
